work: The Self-Disclosure of Jesus: The Modern Debate About the Messianic Consciousness, 1926
edition: New York: George H. Doran Company, 1926 (archive.org scan; no ISBN seen)
chapter_or_section: Section under running head 'STRATEGIC IMPORTANCE' (chapter title not checked)
quote_orig: Lastly the Messianic consciousness is most intimately interwoven with the specifically religious position the Messiah occupies between God and man. It includes at bottom his right to receive worship and his identification with God. These highest of claims are inseparable from it.
context_before: Vos has just argued that stripping Jesus of his Messianic character would also remove the Gospel's ideas of atonement and regeneration. The paragraph that follows turns to the Messianic consciousness of Jesus.
what_it_says: Vos says the Messianic consciousness of Jesus includes his right to receive worship and his identification with God, and that these claims are inseparable from it.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus himself speaks or acts as YHWH / claims divine identity
scholar_qualification: Vos does not cite a saying of Jesus for this on these pages; he argues from the nature of the office as Jesus held it. He says the title to deity and worship 'are not given with the Messiahship as such' (p.27), and on p.28 concedes it is 'logically quite possible' to separate the two 'in the abstract'. He is writing against modern denials of the Messianic consciousness, so this is his theological reading, not a neutral historical-critical conclusion.
limits: Read in archive.org OCR and checked against the scan image (PDF pages 32 and 33, printed pp. 26 and 27). The sentence crosses the page break onto p.27 (after a running head). Book is US public domain (1926). Later chapters, including the Son of Man discussion, not checked for this item.

work: The Self-Disclosure of Jesus: The Modern Debate About the Messianic Consciousness, 1926
edition: New York: George H. Doran Company, 1926 (archive.org scan; no ISBN seen)
chapter_or_section: Section under running head 'STRATEGIC IMPORTANCE' (chapter title not checked)
quote_orig: But we are not dealing with Messiahship in the abstract. Our concern is with that specific type of the office which is present in the consciousness of Jesus. Here the indispensableness of strictly divine prerogatives in order to the adequate exercise of its functions springs into view.
context_before: Vos contrasts the abstract Jewish-pattern Messiah, who could be 'the representative of God without investing Him with divine attributes', with the Messiah in Jesus' own consciousness. The sentence before the quote says 'we are not dealing with Messiahship in the abstract.'
what_it_says: Vos argues that the Messianic office as Jesus conceived it could not be exercised without strictly divine prerogatives, because it concerns the spiritual relationship between God and humanity.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus himself speaks or acts as YHWH / claims divine identity
scholar_qualification: This is Vos's inference from the spiritualised character of the office as he reads it, not a quoted saying. On p.28 he grants that affirming the deity of Jesus and his consciousness of it can in logic be held apart from Messianic consciousness, and calls the reverse case 'practically this is a negligible concession'. He treats the deity claim as implied by the office, not as a separate explicit claim by Jesus.
limits: Checked against the scan image of printed p.27 (PDF page 33). Read in OCR first. Other statements on pp.28-29 not checked here.

work: Jesus and God in the Gospel of Mark: Unity and Distinction, PhD thesis, 2011
edition: Unpublished PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh (title page dated 2011; repository file 2012); repository handle 1842/6432; no publisher
chapter_or_section: Discussion of Mark 14:61-62 (the trial); this is footnote 106 (chapter number not checked)
quote_orig: But in the absence of any early, unambiguous evidence that Christ was thought to be enthroned on a separate throne, and in the light of that at least three different NT traditions clearly shared the notion of Christ sitting on the divine throne (Revelation, Hebrews, Matthew; see Hannah, “Throne,” 80), the balance seems to tip toward the view that the Markan Jesus claims the divine throne.
context_before: Johansson argues that Jesus' answer at the trial (Mark 14:62) would have been heard as an encroachment on divine privileges. Footnote 106 addresses whether the 'heavenly throne' is a second throne or God's own throne.
what_it_says: Johansson concludes that the evidence tips toward the Markan Jesus claiming God's own throne at his trial.
claim_supported: (B) the Gospel writers or earliest Christians portray Jesus as sharing YHWH's unique identity
scholar_qualification: The thesis is about the Markan Jesus as Mark portrays him, not the historical Jesus' own words. In the same footnote Johansson cites D. Hannah, who thinks the evidence is 'too ambiguous to allow any decision'; the footnote is his own judgement ('seems to tip toward'). In the main text he calls the phrase 'ego eimi' ambiguous in itself.
limits: Read from the PDF's own text layer (born-digital thesis), not checked against a page image. Footnote numbers removed from the quote only (none inside the quoted sentence). Thesis has a copyright notice requiring credit for quotation; full bibliographic details are in the item edition field. No cover (unpublished thesis).

work: A Narrative Analysis of Mark's Use of the Shema, 2026
edition: Perichoresis 24.1 (2026): 56-72, Emanuel University of Oradea; DOI 10.2478/perc-2026-0004; open access (Sciendo)
chapter_or_section: Trial section on Mark 14:61-62, near the end of the article (section heading not checked)
quote_orig: The question of whether Jesus considered himself the Christ Son of the Blessed One, the use of ego eimi in this climactic scene, and the description of Jesus as the Son of Man coming in the clouds all lend credence to the reading that Jesus was revealing his divinity in this trial.
context_before: Hicks argues from Daniel 7 that the Son of Man who is served and who rides the clouds is a divine figure, and that what is said of him is later said of God. He then states his conclusion about the trial.
what_it_says: Hicks says the trial questions, the 'I am' answer and the Son of Man coming on the clouds together support reading Jesus as revealing his divinity in the trial.
claim_supported: (B) the Gospel writers or earliest Christians portray Jesus as sharing YHWH's unique identity; (A) only as Mark's presentation of Jesus' trial words
scholar_qualification: Hicks is reading Mark's narrative (his conclusion: 'Mark presents Jesus as understanding himself to be divine'), not the historical Jesus. He reports the alternatives: Marcus's 'quasi-divine' agent reading and Kirk's agent reading (p.63), and says he argues against Marcus. He also notes 'ego eimi' can be a plain phrase of identification (earlier in the trial discussion; page not checked). Academic post and standing not checked.

work: Jesus and God in the Gospel of Mark: Unity and Distinction, PhD thesis, 2011
edition: Unpublished PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh (title page dated 2011; repository file 2012); repository handle 1842/6432; no publisher
chapter_or_section: Discussion of Mark 2:1-12 (forgiveness of sins), section on 2:10
quote_orig: These words cannot imply that Jesus is given an authority to merely offer God’s forgiveness. They ascribe to Jesus himself power to forgive sins in an absolute sense. This is clear from the close parallel between Jesus’ saying and the accusation of the scribes.
context_before: Johansson argues that the scribes object not to a prophetic claim but to Jesus acting like God himself by personally forgiving the paralytic. The quote then gives his reading of Jesus' own words in Mark 2:10.
what_it_says: Johansson reads Jesus' forgiveness in Mark 2:10 as Jesus himself exercising God's own authority to forgive sins, not as delegated authority.
claim_supported: (B) the Gospel writers or earliest Christians portray Jesus as sharing YHWH's unique identity
scholar_qualification: This is a reading of the Markan Jesus, not a historical claim. Johansson acknowledges that Pesch and Marcus read 'on earth' as a contrast with God's heavenly forgiveness (footnote 18) and argues against that reading. He says Mark 'maintains' both Jesus' divinity and Israel's monotheism; his reading is about how Mark presents it.
limits: Read from the PDF's own text layer, not checked against a page image. No footnote markers inside the quoted sentence.

edition: London: Macmillan, 1958 (reprint 1959) per catalogue records; quoted in I. Howard Marshall, 'The Development of Christology in the Early Church', Tyndale Bulletin (year not confirmed; doi 10.53751/001c.30684)
chapter_or_section: Quoted in Marshall's discussion of the teaching of Jesus (Taylor chapter not identified)
page: 186 per Marshall's footnote 4 ('op. cit. 186'); attribution of that short citation not certain
quote_orig: His consciousness of Sonship was gained through the knowledge that God was His Father, mediated by prayer and communion with Him in a process of growth and development which begins before the opening of the historic ministry and is consummated in decisive experiences of revelation and intuition. It is upon this historical foundation that Christological thinking must build.
context_before: Marshall writes that the idea of divine Sonship goes back to Jesus himself and quotes Taylor's words beginning 'Within the limitations of the human life of Jesus' (printed p.77, not quoted here). The next sentence, on p.78, is the quote here.
what_it_says: Taylor says Jesus' consciousness of Sonship came through knowing God as his Father, through prayer and communion, in a developing human life, and that Christology must build on this historical foundation.

scholar_qualification: Taylor's claim is about Jesus' consciousness of 'Sonship' 'within the limitations of the human life', not an explicit claim to deity. Marshall describes Taylor's Christology as 'a kenotic type' and reports that recent scholarship denies that Jesus spoke of himself as the Son of God (p.78). Marshall is not endorsing Taylor here; he is reporting him. The page 186 attribution is uncertain.
